title: NEONOIRE
description: The opening scenes, first draft (September 2026): 7 scenes and 65 numbered shots from a Kanda backstreet to a detectives' room three days later. The screenplay tab carries the draft page by page; the storyboard is generated in passes of ten keyframes, with Mara and Vera held to their continuity sheets. Tokyo as a memory that is still happening — sodium orange against sick fluorescent green, cold patient rain, and nothing explained.

acts.title: The opening — Kanda to the detectives' room
acts.description: Seven scenes from the first draft's opening: a backstreet in Kanda at night, a small bar, Vera's apartment three days later, and a police station that already knows Mara's name. 65 numbered shots; every frame is a draft study, not approved coverage.

parts.title: Kanda, night
parts.description: The cold open and the bar: the killing, the key, and the notebook that leaves with them.

parts.title: Three days later
parts.description: Vera's apartment: two cups, one photograph, an answerphone message, and a blue umbrella that is still bone dry.

parts.title: The police station
parts.description: A missing-person report, an interview in Japanese, and a drawer that closes on a wet purse.

scenes.title: The backstreet
scenes.description: Cold open. Rain in a Kanda backstreet. Mara declines her sister's call, ducks into the doorway of a closed barbershop, and watches two masked men shoot an old man without hurrying — then kneels beside him and takes a coin-locker key out of his hand. BOARDED — 18 shots. The draft's own scene 1; nothing is explained, and nobody names the key.
scenes.lightingNotes: The vending machine is the brightest source in the film's first minute. Sodium orange street lamps, one cold white vending machine, green fluorescent spill at the corner. No white beams in frame, ever.

scenes.title: The small bar
scenes.description: Continuous. Mara hides behind the far end of the counter with the key in her fist. Two pairs of wet black shoes come in softly, ask where is he, and shoot the journalist on the far side of the counter while the television audience laughs. The notebook leaves with them. BOARDED — 10 shots, ending on the blue TV glow and the title card.
scenes.lightingNotes: Amber bottle shelves, the CRT's blue flicker on the ceiling, and the open back door's pale light. No overhead light is ever switched on.

scenes.title: Three days later
scenes.description: SUPER: THREE DAYS LATER. An old four-story block squeezed between newer buildings, laundry left out and getting rained on, a train sliding past behind it — and one window on the third floor lit. BOARDED — 4 shots.
scenes.lightingNotes: Blue hour with practical sodium beginning at street level and the single warm window on the third floor. Rain in the air; no direct sun, no golden hour.

scenes.title: Vera's apartment
scenes.description: Continuous. Vera calls her sister and gets the recording: I'm not angry anymore, you left your umbrella, you'll get soaked, just call me. The television murmurs rain for the rest of the week, two cups sit on the table for one person and the photograph of Jack and his two small daughters holds the room — then she takes Mara's bone-dry blue umbrella and goes out. BOARDED — 10 shots.
scenes.lightingNotes: Flat grey rain light from the window, the CRT's cold glow on the ceiling, one lamp. The framed photograph is the only saturated warm colour in the frame.

scenes.title: The front counter
scenes.description: Night. Vera reports her sister missing, umbrella dripping on the linoleum. A young officer takes her details with polite boredom until the name Mara Voss reaches his monitor; he looks at it a moment too long, turns away, and makes a quiet phone call. He comes back politer. BOARDED — 8 shots.
scenes.lightingNotes: Ceiling fluorescent tubes, one visibly flickering, plus the flat monitor's glow on his face. No sodium in here; the station is its own climate.

scenes.title: The interview room
scenes.description: Moments later. Detective Ishida sets a paper cup of tea in front of Vera and offers her English. She answers in Japanese. He asks where she grew up, when she last saw her sister, whether the name Kanda means anything — and gets: three days ago, we had dinner, normal. He gives her his card and tells her to call at any hour. BOARDED — 9 shots.
scenes.lightingNotes: One ceiling fixture and the frosted window's blue-grey rain light; the paper cup is the only warm note. No flicker in this room.

scenes.title: The detectives' room
scenes.description: Continuous. Alone in the detectives' room, Ishida opens his bottom drawer: sealed in an evidence bag, Mara's purse — the torn strap coiled beside it, still damp. He looks at it a long moment. Closes the drawer. On the wall, the clock runs a minute fast. BOARDED — 6 shots.
scenes.lightingNotes: Humming fluorescent rows, the desk lamp over the drawer, the radio's green dial. The evidence bag is lit plainly, like an exhibit.

frames.title: Backstreet
frames.description: A narrow street of shuttered shops that could belong to any year of the last forty. Hand-painted signs, tangled wires overhead, wet black asphalt, and at the corner the old vending machine throwing cold white light across the road with rain falling through it in columns. Nobody in frame.
frames.mood: Wide, patient and wet; the city does the lighting, and the violence is ordinary.

notes.title: The look — the draft's own words
notes.content:
>THE LOOK<

Tokyo as a memory that is still happening.

The city in this film belongs to no single year. Pay phones beside smartphones. Boxy CRT televisions glowing in shop windows. Showa-era vending machines humming on empty corners beneath new glass towers. None of it is ever commented on. It is simply how the world is.

LIGHT. The city lights the characters, not the sky: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, fluorescent tubes. Sodium orange against a sick fluorescent green. Soft halation around every light, blacks slightly crushed. It should look like film, and feel like something remembered.

RAIN. Never glamorous. No lightning, no storms. Cold, steady, patient rain that turns the streets black and reflective.

CAMERA. Wide and patient. Close-ups are rare, so they count. We watch people inside the city, not apart from it.

SOUND. Real Tokyo sounds, placed slightly wrong: a crossing melody for an empty street, a television laughing in an empty room. Music arrives late, and sparingly.

OTHER LIVES. There is always a sign of other people -- a lit window, a radio through a wall, laundry overhead. Every private moment happens among thousands of others.

!NOTHING IS EXPLAINED.

LANGUAGE. The Voss sisters speak English to each other. Dialogue marked (in Japanese) is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English.

REFERENCE POINTS. Ozu's TOKYO STORY for restraint. KOWLOON GENERIC ROMANCE and the 1997 illustrated Kowloon Walled City panoramas for density, texture and memory.

notes.title: Continuity — the Voss family, and everyone else
notes.content:
**Mara Voss (24)** and **Vera Voss (29)** are both American, both blonde with pale blue eyes, and they must read as sisters while still being told apart at a glance: Mara's hair is longer, wavier and soaked flat for the whole opening; Vera's is shoulder length with a fringe and never wet — she is inside, or under cover, or has the umbrella.

Wardrobe is locked per sheet:
- Mara: indigo denim jacket, heather-grey tee, black jeans, white trainers, black cord necklace, small studs. Soaked from scene 1 until she is behind the bar counter.
- Vera: charcoal wool coat over a cream high-neck knit, navy trousers, brown ankle boots, gold ring on the right hand, black strap watch. Carries Mara's pale blue umbrella — bone dry in the apartment, dripping on police linoleum.

Jack Voss, the girls' father, exists in this opening only inside one framed photograph on Vera's shelf: a rumpled suit, a smile, both daughters' hands in his, a Tokyo noodle-shop sign behind them, twenty years ago, colours gone warm and faded. He is the only saturated warm colour in the film so far and he is never spoken about.

The men in masks are never given faces: eyes above the mask, gloved hands, wet black shoes. The old man and the journalist are unnamed on purpose. Detective Ishida and the young officer are the only police with faces, and the young officer's face changes after the monitor does.

notes.title: Language — English, Japanese, and the subtitles
notes.content:
The Voss sisters speak **English** to each other — including on the phone, including the answerphone message Vera cannot bring herself to answer.

Dialogue marked *(in Japanese)* is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English, and it is never used for local colour: Mara's Japanese is halting and she is understood just barely; Vera's is fluent, careful and slightly formal, learned as a child and relearned as an adult; Ishida's English is excellent and she refuses it anyway, which is the only line either of them draws in the interview room. The old man's "twenty years" and "don't let them have it" are Japanese, and the masked man's two position reports are Japanese into a radio.

The audience is never told what the key opens, what the position reports are counting towards, or why the journalist had a notebook. Nothing is explained — that is the film's rule, and it is also the workspace's.

notes.title: What the keyframes are, and what they are not
notes.content:
Every frame in this storyboard is a **draft AI study** standing in for a shot that has not been photographed. They are generated in passes of ten, in screenplay order, from the boards in `docs/neonoire/scenes/` with the cast sheets attached as references.

They are useful for: framing, lens, blocking, light direction, wardrobe continuity, and seeing whether the scene plays in order in the animatic.

They are not: approved coverage, a lighting plan, a cast approval, or a licence to stop checking. Faces drift between passes more than anything else — if a study of Mara or Vera does not match her sheet, mark the frame **Needs review** and regenerate it. Each frame's notes carry the pass it came from.

brainstorm.title: The key
brainstorm.content: A small numbered key on a worn plastic tag — a coin-locker key, pressed into Mara's palm by a dying man with the words don't let them have it. Never explained in the opening, and the reason she is running.

brainstorm.title: Two positions
brainstorm.content: First position done. Moving to second. Second position done. The men work to a list and the film never shows who writes it; the journalist in the bar was already on it, and he had a notebook.

brainstorm.title: The city that lights them
brainstorm.content: Sodium orange against sick fluorescent green: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, a CRT's blue flicker. The sky never does the work, and the rain turns everything black and reflective.

brainstorm.title: Mara, running
brainstorm.content: Twenty-four, American, soaked flat, no umbrella, arms folded, halting Japanese. She declines a call, chooses not to run when every instinct says to, and takes the key anyway.

brainstorm.title: Vera's two cups
brainstorm.content: Three days later: one cup of cold tea, one empty and clean, set out as though someone is expected. The answerphone message is an apology, and the umbrella in the stand has never been wet.

brainstorm.content: The station is a decade out of step: faded posters, a fax machine beside a flat monitor, and a clock that runs a minute fast. Ishida gives Vera his card at any hour and then closes a drawer on her sister's purse.

Title: NEONOIRE
Credit: Written by
Author: [Your Name]
Draft date: First Draft - Opening Scenes
Contact: September 2026

===

>THE LOOK<

Tokyo as a memory that is still happening.

The city in this film belongs to no single year. Pay phones beside smartphones. Boxy CRT televisions glowing in shop windows. Showa-era vending machines humming on empty corners beneath new glass towers. None of it is ever commented on. It is simply how the world is.

LIGHT. The city lights the characters, not the sky: vending machines, shop signs, train windows, fluorescent tubes. Sodium orange against a sick fluorescent green. Soft halation around every light, blacks slightly crushed. It should look like film, and feel like something remembered.

RAIN. Never glamorous. No lightning, no storms. Cold, steady, patient rain that turns the streets black and reflective.

CAMERA. Wide and patient. Close-ups are rare, so they count. We watch people inside the city, not apart from it.

SOUND. Real Tokyo sounds, placed slightly wrong: a crossing melody for an empty street, a television laughing in an empty room. Music arrives late, and sparingly.

OTHER LIVES. There is always a sign of other people -- a lit window, a radio through a wall, laundry overhead. Every private moment happens among thousands of others.

!NOTHING IS EXPLAINED.

LANGUAGE. The Voss sisters speak English to each other. Dialogue marked (in Japanese) is spoken in Japanese and subtitled in English.

REFERENCE POINTS. Ozu's TOKYO STORY for restraint. KOWLOON GENERIC ROMANCE and the 1997 illustrated Kowloon Walled City panoramas for density, texture and memory.

===

FADE IN:

EXT. BACKSTREET, KANDA - NIGHT

Rain. Not a storm. Just cold, steady, patient rain.

A narrow street of shuttered shops that could belong to any year of the last forty. Hand-painted signs. Tangled wires overhead. At the corner, an old vending machine throws cold white light across the wet asphalt, rain falling through it in columns.

Its HUM is the loudest thing here.

MARA VOSS (24), American, walks fast, arms folded, no umbrella. Hair soaked flat. She has been crying, or she is about to.

Her phone BUZZES. The screen: VERA.

She looks at it. Lets it ring. Declines.

It buzzes again at once. VERA.

MARA
(to the phone)
Not tonight.

She switches it off and shoves it into her purse.

The rain thickens. She ducks into the recessed doorway of a closed barbershop, its striped pole dark and still, and presses back into the shadow. Going nowhere.

Somewhere nearby, a pedestrian crossing CHIMES its old melody for an empty intersection. Over and over. No one crosses.

Footsteps. Hurried. Uneven.

An OLD MAN (70s) in a cheap raincoat, one hand pressed to his side as if something is hidden there. He keeps looking back.

He passes Mara's doorway without seeing her.

Headlights sweep the wet street. A black sedan rolls in and stops without hurry.

Two MEN step out. Black clothes. Masks. They don't run.

The old man stops. He doesn't turn around. He seems to know there is no point.

OLD MAN
(in Japanese; to himself)
Twenty years.

A suppressed SHOT. Flat and ordinary, like a door closing.

The old man folds to his knees, then onto his side in the black water.

In the doorway, Mara has both hands over her mouth.

One of the masked men touches his earpiece.

MASKED MAN
(in Japanese)
First position done. Moving to second.

They get back in the car. It pulls away, unhurried. Taillights smear red across the road and are gone.

Rain. The vending machine hum. The crossing melody, still playing for no one.

Mara doesn't move.

Then the old man COUGHS.

She stares. He is still alive.

Every instinct says run. She doesn't. She steps out into the rain and kneels beside him.

MARA
It's okay -- I'll get someone --
(in halting Japanese)
Ambulance. I'll call. Ambulance.

She fumbles for her phone. Switched off. Her hands shake too hard to turn it on.

The old man grips her wrist, stronger than he should be. He presses something small and cold into her palm and folds her fingers around it.

OLD MAN
(in Japanese)
Don't let them have it.

Mara's lips move, working through the words. She understands. Just.

MARA
(in halting Japanese)
Have what? I don't --

His grip loosens. His eyes stay open, on nothing.

She opens her hand.

.INSERT - THE KEY

A small numbered key on a worn plastic tag. A coin-locker key.

.BACK TO SCENE

Headlights. Coming back.

Mara runs.

Her purse strap snags on the barbershop pole and tears. The purse drops into a puddle behind her. She doesn't stop.

The sedan pulls up beside the body. One masked man gets out and searches the old man's coat, methodically. Nothing.

His flashlight drifts across the street -- and stops on the purse lying in the water.

CUT TO:

INT. SMALL BAR, KANDA - CONTINUOUS

Six stools and a counter. Shelves of bottles glowing amber. On a high shelf, an old CRT television plays a late-night variety show, sound low. Rain drums on the roof.

No one behind the counter. A door to the back stands half open; someone back there is moving crates.

In the corner, a JOURNALIST (40s), an untouched beer in front of him, a notebook closed beside it. He checks his watch. Checks the door.

The door BANGS open. Mara, soaked, too out of breath to speak.

The journalist glances up, startled. Then away. Not his business.

Mara stands dripping, looking for somewhere to go. There is nowhere. She slips behind the far end of the counter and crouches out of sight of the door, her back against the shelves.

She opens her hand. The key. She closes it again.

FROM THE FLOOR, we see only what she sees: the underside of the counter, a crate of empty bottles, the journalist's shoes beneath his stool, and the TV's flickering blue glow on the ceiling.

The door opens again. Softly, this time.

Two pairs of black shoes step inside. Wet. Silent.

The journalist's shoes shift. He stands.

JOURNALIST (O.S.)
(in Japanese)
Where is he?

No answer.

Two suppressed SHOTS.

The stool tips over. The journalist hits the floor on the far side of the counter. We see only his hand.

On the TV, the studio audience LAUGHS.

One pair of shoes crosses to the body. Pages rustle. The notebook, taken.

In the back room, the crate-moving stops.

A pair of shoes turns toward the half-open door. Waits. Nothing moves.

MASKED MAN (O.S.)
(in Japanese; into radio)
Second position done.

The shoes leave. The door swings shut.

Mara stays exactly where she is. She is shaking so hard the bottles in the crate beside her begin to CLINK. She presses her hand flat against them to make them stop.

The TV audience laughs again.

HOLD on her face in the blue TV glow: a young woman who has just understood that this was not random.

>CUT TO BLACK.

Over black: RAIN.

>NEONOIRE<

>MAIN TITLES<

EXT. VERA'S APARTMENT BUILDING - DUSK

SUPER: "THREE DAYS LATER"

An old four-story apartment block squeezed between newer buildings. Laundry left out on a balcony, getting rained on. A train slides past on the elevated line behind it, windows lit, and the whole building trembles faintly.

One window on the third floor is lit.

INT. VERA'S APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

Small and tidy. Grey light through rain-streaked glass. A smartphone on the table; an old boxy television in the corner. Nothing here quite belongs to one decade.

By the door, in the umbrella stand: a pale blue umbrella. Bone dry.

On a shelf, one framed photograph, its colors gone warm and faded. A Tokyo street, twenty years ago. An American man in a rumpled suit, smiling, holding the hands of two small girls: VERA (9), serious, and MARA (4), mid-laugh. Behind them, the sign of a noodle shop.

VERA VOSS (29) sits at the low table. Two cups. Hers holds cold tea. The other is empty and clean, set out as though someone is expected.

Her phone lies face up in front of her. She calls. Waits.

MARA (V.O.)
(recorded; bright)
It's Mara. You know what to do.

BEEP.

Vera opens her mouth. For a moment, nothing.

VERA
It's me again.
(beat)
I'm not angry anymore. I wasn't really angry then, either. I just --
(stops herself)
You left your umbrella. You'll get soaked.
(beat)
Just call me. You don't have to say anything. Just call, so I know.

She hangs up.

The old television murmurs to itself.

WEATHER ANNOUNCER (ON TV)
(in Japanese)
...rain continuing through the rest of the week...

She looks at the umbrella by the door. At the clean, empty cup. At the photograph.

She stands. Puts on her coat. Hesitates at the door.

Then she takes the blue umbrella. Mara's umbrella.

CUT TO:

INT. POLICE STATION, FRONT COUNTER - NIGHT

Fluorescent tubes, one of them flickering. A long counter. Faded posters about pickpockets and traffic safety. An old fax machine beside a new flat monitor. A wall clock that runs a minute fast.

Vera stands at the counter, the closed blue umbrella dripping onto the linoleum.

A YOUNG OFFICER takes her details with polite boredom. Vera's Japanese is fluent, but careful and slightly formal -- learned as a child, relearned as an adult.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese)
Your sister's age?

VERA
(in Japanese)
Twenty-four.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese)
Adults sometimes go away for a few days. Especially foreigners. It's usually --

VERA
(in Japanese)
She doesn't. Not without telling me.

He types the name. ON THE MONITOR: MARA VOSS.

He stops typing.

He looks at the screen a moment too long. Then he picks up the desk phone and turns away from her.

YOUNG OFFICER
(in Japanese; quietly, into phone)
Yes. That name. Yes -- the sister is here now.

He hangs up. His manner has changed. Politer.

YOUNG OFFICER (CONT'D)
(in Japanese)
Someone will be right with you.

Vera looks at him. He doesn't meet her eyes.

INT. POLICE STATION, INTERVIEW ROOM - MOMENTS LATER

Small. A table, two chairs, a box of tissues nobody has touched in years. Rain on a frosted window.

DETECTIVE ISHIDA (50s) sets a paper cup of tea in front of Vera. Gentle. Unhurried. Tired, in a way that looks like decency.

ISHIDA
You must be cold.

His English is excellent.

VERA
(in Japanese)
I speak Japanese.

ISHIDA
Of course. But this is a difficult thing. It is easier in your own language.

A small beat. She lets it go.

VERA
Is something wrong? He looked at the screen, and then --

ISHIDA
Nothing is wrong. We just like to take care with these things.
(sits)
Voss. You grew up here?

VERA
Until I was nine.

ISHIDA
It must have changed very much.

VERA
Not as much as I thought.

He smiles at that, as if it pleases him.

ISHIDA
When did you last see your sister?

VERA
Three days ago. At my apartment. We had dinner.

ISHIDA
And how did she seem?

Vera hesitates.

VERA
Normal.

Ishida waits, kindly, as if he knows there is more. She doesn't give it.

ISHIDA
Did she ever mention Kanda? Friends there? Work?

VERA
Kanda? No. Why Kanda?

ISHIDA
We ask about many places.

VERA
You asked about one.

A small pause. Ishida smiles mildly, as if she has caught him in something harmless.

ISHIDA
You would make a good detective.
(gently)
Go home, Miss Voss. Keep your phone on. If she calls, call me first. Any hour.

He slides his card across the table. She takes it. Stands. Picks up the blue umbrella.

VERA
She will call.

ISHIDA
I'm sure she will.

She goes. The door closes behind her.

Ishida sits alone a moment, looking at the untouched tea.

INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Rows of cluttered desks under humming fluorescent light. Most are empty at this hour. A radio plays low somewhere.

Ishida sits at his desk and opens the bottom drawer.

.INSERT - THE DRAWER

Sealed in a clear evidence bag: Mara's purse. The torn strap coiled beside it. Still damp.

.BACK TO SCENE

He looks at it a long moment. Closes the drawer.

On the wall, the clock runs a minute fast.
